extracted.intended_audience: owners/operators of combustion turbine EGUs, power-sector industry stakeholders, and federal/state regulators
extracted.subtask_short: NSPS BSER evaluation for combustion turbines
extracted.subtask_description: EPA's rulemaking preamble evaluating the Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) for new and reconstructed stationary combustion turbines (base load and intermediate load), including consideration of CCS, hydrogen co-firing, alternate technologies, compliance timelines, costs, and applicability criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate demonstration and deployability within compliance timeframe
rubrics_metrics.description: Under CAA section 111, for a control technology to qualify as the BSER, the EPA must demonstrate that it is 'adequately demonstrated' for affected sources and must show that the industry can deploy the technology at scale in the compliance timeframe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Agency may provide lead time to enable industry deployment; lead time is consistent with caselaw (e.g., Portland Cement v. Ruckelshaus). The fact that a technology is not already in widespread commercial use does not preclude it from being 'adequately demonstrated' if deployment within the compliance timeframe is feasible. EPA's provision of lead time is evidence of meeting statutory obligations, not evidence against adequate demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeline and compliance date for CCS on new base load combustion turbines
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA bases the timeline for CCS on new combustion turbines on the extended S&L capture plant schedule (7 years) and is finalizing a compliance date of January 1, 2032 for base load combustion turbine EGUs to meet the phase 2 standard (90% capture CCS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale includes similarity of CCS component development timelines to coal-fired EGUs, the absence of state-plan processes allowing earlier substantial work, and allowance for turbines that did not include CCS in original design to have later compliance. EPA considered but rejected a 2035 delay for phase 2; the chosen date aligns with deployment capacity and reduces overlap demands on CCS and pipeline construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: CCS as BSER (readiness and implementation requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Carbon capture and storage (CCS) is determined by EPA to be clearly adequately demonstrated and ripe for wider implementation as a BSER pathway for applicable combustion turbines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploying CCS requires building capture facilities, CO2 transport pipelines, and development of sequestration sites. EPA's assessment considers design, planning, permitting, engineering, and construction steps and allows lead time for industry to develop and deploy CCS at scale. EPA assumes component timelines for coal-fired EGUs are similar to those for new/reconstructed base load combustion turbines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low-GHG hydrogen co-firing as BSER — eligibility criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA proposed a BSER pathway consisting of hydrogen co-firing (e.g., 30% by volume by 2032 for intermediate load; optionally 30% by 2032 and 96% by 2038 for base load), but did not finalize it because projected costs and availability were uncertain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For hydrogen co-firing to qualify as BSER, EPA required (proposed) that: (a) turbines' capability to co-fire hydrogen be adequately demonstrated, and (b) there be a reasonable expectation that necessary quantities of low-GHG hydrogen would be nationally available by target years at reasonable cost. EPA conducted additional analysis after comments and found higher estimated delivered hydrogen costs and uncertainty about nationwide availability, which were key factors in not finalizing hydrogen co-firing as BSER.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed definition of low-GHG hydrogen (not finalized)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA proposed to define low-GHG hydrogen as hydrogen produced with emissions of less than 0.45 kg CO2e/kg H2, from well-to-gate, aligned with the highest tier of the IRC section 45V hydrogen production tax credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA solicited comment on this definition and alternatives but did not finalize a definition because it is not finalizing hydrogen co-firing as a BSER pathway and chose not to lock in its own definition while Treasury and other processes are developing verification/measurement protocols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that hydrogen used for compliance be low-GHG
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA proposed requiring that hydrogen co-fired for compliance be low-GHG hydrogen to avoid an outcome where a GHG control strategy increases overall lifecycle emissions, but chose not to finalize such a requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA still emphasizes the importance of co-firing only low-GHG hydrogen for true GHG reductions. Reasons for not finalizing the requirement include nascent market practices, forthcoming Treasury parameters for IRC section 45V, ongoing development of accounting/verification protocols, and potential unhelpful regulatory prescriptiveness at this time. EPA expects market and policy incentives (IIJA, IRA, tax credits) will encourage low-GHG hydrogen uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hydrogen production lifecycle emissions (well-to-gate) as an evaluation factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessments of hydrogen co-firing must consider GHG emissions associated with hydrogen production methods (well-to-gate), because hydrogen production methods vary widely in their GHG profiles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA notes that combustion is zero-GHG emitting but production can range from low to high emissions. Evaluating net GHG benefits of co-firing requires accounting for production emissions, and stakeholders typically characterize hydrogen by production pathway. This lifecycle consideration informed the proposed low-GHG definition and the Agency's caution about relying on hydrogen absent robust measurement/verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost and availability analysis for low-GHG hydrogen (price assumptions and uncertainty)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's BSER determination for hydrogen depended on modeled delivered cost and projected availability; revised modeling used a delivered price of $1.15/kg (final baseline and policy cases), higher than some prior assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA referenced DOE, McKinsey, BloombergNEF, Rhodium estimates and Treasury/regulatory uncertainty; higher estimated costs and uncertain availability across the nation were principal reasons for not finalizing hydrogen co-firing as BSER. Tax credits (IRC section 45V) and infrastructure funding affect economics; competition for hydrogen across sectors influences power-sector willingness to pay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial capture CCS evaluation criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Partial capture CCS was not determined to be BSER because it yields lower emission reductions and, in general, higher costs compared to high-capture designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA explains that 90% capture removes very high absolute emissions and gains economies of scale; partial capture would capture much less and could disqualify a project from IRC section 45Q tax credits if capture design rates don't meet the equivalent threshold (e.g., 75% of baseline emission rate by mass), reducing financial returns and making partial capture comparatively more expensive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combined Heat and Power (CHP) suitability criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: CHP was evaluated and not selected as BSER because a critical requirement for CHP is primary generation of useful thermal output to a proximate thermal host with consistent demand; this limits applicability and scale for large EGUs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constraints include difficulty locating a sufficiently large thermal host, typical thermal hosts supporting at most several hundred MW (limiting EGU size), geographic limitations, reliance on continuous operation of the thermal host (risking compliance), and financing difficulties (host might demand discounted pricing). These practical constraints make CHP generally unsuitable as the BSER for large new combustion turbine EGUs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybrid power plant evaluation criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Hybrid power plants (e.g., integrating concentrating solar thermal with a fossil-fired EGU) were considered but not chosen as BSER; relevant evaluation factors include capital and O&M costs, efficiency benefits, and integration requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits include lower incremental capital/O&M for non-emitting generation by using existing fossil-plant equipment and improved generation efficiency when low-quality solar thermal steam is upgraded in the fossil boiler/HRSG. Primary incremental costs include mirrors, piping, and a steam turbine 10–20% larger than a fossil-only EGU. Applicability and cost-effectiveness depend on site-specific integration opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tax credit eligibility and incentives as determinants of BSER viability
rubrics_metrics.description: Availability and structure of tax credits (e.g., IRC sections 45Q for sequestration, 45V for hydrogen production) materially affect cost-effectiveness and the EPA's assessment of whether a technology is viable as BSER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA aligned proposed definitions and assumptions with tax-credit tiers, and noted that eligibility criteria (e.g., capture rates tied to 45Q) influence returns. Uncertainty in Treasury regulations implementing credits and in how credits apply to delivered vs. production costs affects EPA's willingness to finalize technology pathways reliant on those incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring, stakeholder engagement, and potential future rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA will monitor development of low-GHG hydrogen industry and other technologies, open non-regulatory dockets, review petitions (e.g., petition to regulate thermochemical hydrogen production), and may reevaluate determinations and promulgate standards in the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA described plans to solicit public comment, develop framing questions for potential regulation of hydrogen production emissions under CAA sections 111/112, consider HAP/criteria pollutant controls for hydrogen production, and use non-regulatory engagement to inform potential future standards. This ongoing monitoring is part of the Agency's approach to avoid locking in premature regulatory definitions or requirements.
